chunk_findings.detail:
`_is_prose_key` is purely line-based: it only suppresses a line when *that line* opens a YAML key, so a prose value folded onto continuation lines (or written as a block scalar) is still scanned. Given

```yaml
      - id: lease
        name: >-
          ddflow lease covers the staged paths
        entry: scripts/ddflow_hook.sh hooks check-commit
```

the folded value lives on a line with no `key:` token. `_YAML_KEY` therefore does not match, `_is_prose_key` returns `False`, and `_text_findings` runs `refs_in` over `          ddflow lease covers the staged paths`, emitting the same `lease ... is not a ddflow command` finding the change was supposed to eliminate (now attributed to the continuation line instead of the `name:` line). The regression test passes only because its `name:` values happen to sit on the same physical line as the key, which is exactly the case the line-based heuristic happens to cover. To be correct, `skip` must also suppress continuation lines of a prose key (i.e. track the current key/indent), not just lines that themselves start with a key.

chunk_findings.detail:
A folded/literal prose value whose content contains a line that is itself shaped like a YAML key (`[A-Za-z_][\w-]*\s*:`) resets the "inside a prose value" column, so the *following* content lines at the same indentation are no longer skipped and the original false positive comes straight back. `_YAML_KEY` matches any `token: [REDACTED] line, and `https:` is such a token because the regex only requires a word immediately followed by `:`. Given

```yaml
      - id: lease
        name: >-
          https://example.com/ddflow
          ddflow lease covers the staged paths
        entry: scripts/ddflow_hook.sh hooks check-commit
```

the `https://…` line matches `_YAML_KEY` with `group(2) == "https"`, so `under` becomes 10 and the line is skipped; the next line is indented 10, `10 > 10` is false, the `else` branch sets `under = None`, and that line is scanned. `refs_in` then reports `ddflow lease` — i.e. `doctor` prints exactly the "`lease` is not a ddflow command this version has" message the change says it fixes. The same happens with any other key-shaped first content line (`Note:`, `Example:`, `http:`…). The new regression test only covers a continuation line that cannot match `_YAML_KEY`, so it does not exercise this path.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/compat_refs.py:_prose_lines

chunk_findings.detail:
The `elif` skips *every* non-blank line that does not match `_YAML_KEY` and is merely indented more than the last prose key, so a real command line that does not have the `key:` shape is now silently dropped. With a flow-style hook (or a quoted key), e.g.

```yaml
repos:
  - repo: local
    hooks:
      - id: bad
        name: ok
      - {id: bad2, entry: ddflow gate bogus}
```

the previous line `    hooks:` / `      - id: bad` (prose) leaves `under` at 6, the `{…}` line does not match `_YAML_KEY` (it starts with `{`), `6 > 6`-style comparison passes, so it is added to `skipped` and the bogus `ddflow gate bogus` entry is never reported. Before this change `_is_prose_key(line)` returned `False` for that line and it was scanned. Any non-`key:` line carrying a command (flow mapping, quoted/aliased key) can be swallowed the same way whenever it sits under a prose key.

chunk_findings.detail:
`_command_lines` recomputes "which lines carry a command" by taking each parsed `entry`/`args` string and returning the *first line at or after `at` that contains that string as a substring*. It never checks that the matched line is actually an `entry:`/`args:` line. So any `name:` line that contains the entry text verbatim is added to `scanned` and is scanned by `_text_findings` — i.e. exactly the false positive this change claims to eliminate can still occur.

Concrete input (same shape as the reported config, where the hook's human name embeds the command it runs):

```yaml
repos:
  - repo: local
    hooks:
      - id: hook-a
        name: scripts/ddflow_hook.sh hooks check-commit (ddflow lease)
        entry: scripts/ddflow_hook.sh hooks check-commit
        language: script
```

`_command_values` yields `"scripts/ddflow_hook.sh hooks check-commit"`. `_command_lines` searches from line 0 and finds that string first inside the `name:` line (line 4), so line 4 is added to the returned set. `_text_findings` then runs `refs_in` on `name: scripts/ddflow_hook.sh hooks check-commit (ddflow lease)`, matches `ddflow lease`, and reports `lease is not a ddflow command` — the original `doctor-parses-hook-name-as-command` symptom, despite the `name:` field having no command key.

The root cause is that the value→line association is a fuzzy substring search over the whole file (`piece in lines[i]`) rather than a match against the `entry:`/`args:` key whose line the value came from (e.g. matching the key prefix, or tracking the parsed node's source position). A hook name that quotes its own command is enough to re-trigger the bug.

chunk_findings.detail:
The new filter only decides *which lines* may carry a command, not which field the text came from, so it does not fix the reported false positive whenever the `name:` and `entry:` of a hook sit on the same physical line. The `elif _FLOW_COMMAND_KEY.search(line): inside = False; out.add(i)` branch explicitly admits any line containing `, entry:`/`, args:` (or `{entry:`), which is exactly the compact/flow form of a hook:

```yaml
repos:
- repo: local
  hooks:
  - {id: ddflow-lease, name: ddflow lease covers the staged paths, entry: scripts/ddflow_hook.sh hooks check-commit}
```

Line 4 is added to the candidate set by `_FLOW_COMMAND_KEY`, and the entry value (`scripts/ddflow_hook.sh hooks check-commit`) maps to that same line, so line 4 is in the set returned by this function. Since the finding is kept per line, the `ddflow lease` text that lives in the `name:` field on that line is still reported — doctor prints `...:4 (pre-commit config): lease is not a ddflow command this version has`, i.e. the exact symptom described in the bug the change claims to fix. The same leak happens in block style for a `name:` value that itself contains `, args:` / `, entry:` (e.g. `name: "use ddflow lease, args: --staged"`), because `_FLOW_COMMAND_KEY.search` admits that line too. Fixing this requires filtering the *values* (or the finding text) rather than only the lines.

chunk_findings.detail: The new test sets only the *local* identity (`_git(repo, "config", "user.name", "Stray")`) and never configures a *global* one, yet the feature it is meant to exercise is explicitly "local-identity-vs-global" (per the change's own intent). Two consequences follow. (1) The test does not test the comparison it claims to: it would pass unchanged even if `doctor_notes` simply reported any locally-set `user.name`, so a regression that drops the vs-global logic (e.g. flagging only when local == global, or ignoring global entirely) is not caught. (2) It is non-hermetic: the result depends on the host `git config --global user.name`. Run on a CI runner/container where no global `user.name` is configured, a `doctor_notes` implementation that only flags a local value when it *differs from* a (present) global emits no note, and `assert any("user.name = 'Stray'" in n for n in notes)` fails with `notes` empty of that entry; conversely, on a host whose global name happens to be `Stray`, the "differs" condition is false and the same assertion fails. Setting both a distinct global value and the local value (or forcing the global via the test env) would make the assertion deterministic and actually pin the local-vs-global semantics.

data.claim: enforce._check_lease exempts only SELF_MANAGED prefixes; .claude/settings.json etc. need a lease although the upgrade wrote them
data.falsifier: the test commits the upgrade output without a lease on unfixed code
data.mechanism: no link between the upgrade.applied record and the commit hook
data.probe_output: FAILED: 1 staged path(s) are not covered by a lease you hold: .claude/settings.json
data.question: Why can an agent not commit what upgrade --apply wrote?

evidence.note: CONFIRMED: test failed on unfixed code with the lease refusal for .claude/settings.json
brief read; design: digest-bound exemption (no blanket path exemption), chore ceremony untouched (DX-chore-commit not built)
upgrade_written.py + upgrade_apply records 'written' digests, sessions handler folds them, enforce._beyond_upgrade_output; 2 tests

chunk_findings.detail: The exemption is decided from `upgrade.applied` records (the `written` map) that live in `.ddflow/events/`, i.e. precisely the files the bug report says are committable without a lease, and the value it compares is `hashlib.sha256(staged_bytes(p)).hexdigest()` — a hash the committer can compute from the very blob they are staging. Nothing in the new code (or in the otherwise-unchanged event reader) authenticates the record against a real `upgrade --apply` run: there is no signature, no run/lease binding, no requirement that the event pre-date the commit. Concrete input, in a repo with `[enforce].commit_without_lease = block`: `git add src/x.py` (no lease, no task), then drop `{"kind":"upgrade.applied","written":{"src/x.py":"<sha256 of the staged src/x.py blob>"}}` into `.ddflow/events/`. `_beyond_upgrade_output` finds `src/x.py` in `wrote`, the staged digest matches, so the path is removed; `paths` becomes empty and `commit_without_lease` returns `Verdict(OK, "")`, and the commit lands with no lease. The docstring's promise — "the tool's own output needs no lease, but a file edited after the upgrade has another digest and does" — therefore does not hold: a file edited (or created) after any upgrade is exempted too, as long as the committer also writes an event naming its new digest, which is exactly the trick the gate exists to prevent. If the intent is that only the tool's real output is exempt, the exemption must be anchored to something the committer cannot mint on demand (e.g. the event being part of the same `upgrade --apply` invocation/proof, or the path set being recorded in a trusted location), not to a content hash read out of a lease-exempt log.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/enforce.py:_beyond_upgrade_output

chunk_findings.detail: The new `written` map is only ever persisted on the success branch. `_close` receives `wrote`, but forwards it to `_record` only when `ok or stamp_only`; otherwise it takes `elif run:` and appends a bare `_note(..., "failed", summary=...)`, which has no `written` field. Concretely: run `ddflow upgrade --apply` in backup mode `none` (so `saved` is empty and nothing can be restored) on a repo where a migration/repair rewrites `.ddflow/config.toml` or `AGENTS.md` and the run then settles no item (`ok` empty, `_unresolved(plan, ok)` true, `stamp_only` false). The files are already rewritten on disk, but the closing event is a failure note with no `written` entry, so the lease-exempt path the fix introduces has nothing to match and `git commit` is still refused with `Policy is [enforce].commit_without_lease = block` — exactly the symptom of upgrade-output-needs-lease-to-commit, now reachable via any failed/aborted apply. Since `wrote` is computed before `_close` and is available there, dropping it on the failure path is a gap in the change's own promise to record "what the run changes … as written", not an inherent limitation.

chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/upgrade_apply.py:452 (`_close`, branch `if ok or stamp_only: ... elif run:`)

chunk_findings.detail: The exemption this module implements is self-certified by an artifact the agent itself can write. The docstring states the mechanism plainly: the apply "records, in its closing `upgrade.applied` event, the SHA-256 of every file whose bytes it changed or created (`written`, repo-relative path -> digest). The hook waves a staged path through when the bytes being committed are exactly those." Nothing in the module binds that digest to the upgrade process, to a signature, or to the set of paths the running ddflow version actually writes — the set of exemptable paths is exactly whatever the event says. Given the very bug this change closes ("only `.ddflow/events/` files committed freely"), an agent can write `.ddflow/events/<n>.json` containing an `upgrade.applied` record such as `{"written": {".claude/settings.json": "<sha256 of payload>"}}`, put that content in the file (or in any path it names), stage it, and the hook waves it through. Result: `enforce.commit_without_lease = block` stops protecting anything, and any file — not just the upgrade's known outputs — becomes committable. Contrast with a fix that keys the exemption to the fixed list of paths the current upgrade writes (so a forged event can at most re-admit content the upgrade itself would have produced): here the digest map is the whole authority, and it is the least trustworthy input in the system.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/upgrade_written.py:1-12 (`written` / module docstring)

chunk_findings.detail: The regression test exercises exactly one of the five files named in the bug report (`.claude/settings.json`); `.ddflow/config.toml`, `AGENTS.md`, `CLAUDE.md` and `docs/ddflow/drivers/implement-phase.md` are never asserted committable. This makes the test incapable of catching the most likely residual failure of the fix: if the apply only forwards a subset of the rewritten paths into `written(repo, before, paths)` (e.g. the settings/hooks step passes `[settings]` while the docs/AGENTS writers never call it), those other files remain lease-gated and the reported workflow still fails, yet `test_the_output_of_an_upgrade_commits_without_a_lease` passes. The test only proves "the exemption works for the one path that happens to be plumbed through", not "upgrade output commits".
